papers.abstract: This research introduces the Theory of Partial Symmetry Enforced Attention Decomposition (PSEAD), a new and rigorous group-theoretic framework designed to seamlessly integrate local symmetry awareness into the core architecture of self-attention mechanisms within Transformer models. We formalize the concept of local permutation subgroup actions on windows of biological data, proving that under such actions, the attention mechanism naturally decomposes into a direct sum of orthogonal irreducible components. Critically, these components are intrinsically aligned with the irreducible representations of the acting permutation subgroup, thereby providing a powerful mathematical basis for disentangling symmetric and asymmetric features. We show that PSEAD offers substantial advantages. These include enhanced generalization capabilities to novel biological motifs exhibiting similar partial symmetries, unprecedented interpretability by allowing direct visualization and analysis of attention contributions from different symmetry channels, and significant computational efficiency gains by focusing representational capacity on relevant symmetric subspaces. Beyond static data analysis, we extend PSEAD's applicability to dynamic biological processes within reinforcement learning paradigms, showcasing its potential to accelerate the discovery and optimization of biologically meaningful policies in complex environments like protein folding and drug discovery. This work lays the groundwork for a new generation of biologically informed, symmetry-aware artificial intelligence models.

papers.title: BERT Learns (and Teaches) Chemistry
papers.research_question: Can attention mechanisms in BERT be used to identify important molecular substructures (functional groups) from SMILES string representations and apply these learned representations to chemical property prediction tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that BERT's attention mechanisms can identify chemically relevant functional groups from SMILES strings without domain heuristics, and that these learned representations can be applied to downstream chemical property prediction tasks.
papers.conclusion: Attention visualization in BERT provides a data-driven method to identify functional groups and important molecular substructures from SMILES strings, offering a potentially useful tool for computational chemistry despite not achieving state-of-the-art performance on downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's attention heads, trained only on SMILES strings, learn to attend to atoms that correspond to known active reaction sites (functional groups) in molecules, even without explicit reaction data.
When fine-tuned on chemical property regression tasks (e.g., solubility), specific attention heads in BERT focus on relevant substructures (e.g., carbon chains for solubility).
Using BERT embeddings as features for graph models (GCN, GAT) on toxicity prediction tasks yields competitive but not state-of-the-art performance compared to canonical atom featurization.
Attention visualization of BERT trained on chemical data can serve as a tool for chemistry practitioners to quickly identify important substructures related to various chemical properties.
papers.limitation:
BERT embeddings did not improve upon the state of the art when used as features for graph models on toxicity prediction; the learned information appears to be a subset of that captured by canonical atom featurization.
Some molecules in the Tox21 dataset contain atoms not present in BERT's vocabulary, which may detract from performance.
Attention heads after fine-tuning on most chemical property tasks (QED, SAS) showed little change from pretraining, except for the solubility task, suggesting the fine-tuning may find a local optimum close to pretraining weights.
future_direction: Using a larger dataset of 96 million molecules from PubMed to train BERT, given that language models thrive with abundant data.
Designing a loss function that penalizes distances between embeddings of different SMILES strings representing the same molecule to force BERT to learn the inherent graphical meaning.
Further investigating the approach of analyzing chemical property-bearing molecular substructures via fine-tuning to make it a more useful tool for chemists.
papers.abstract: Modern computational organic chemistry is becoming increasingly data-driven. There remain a large number of important unsolved problems in this area such as product prediction given reactants, drug discovery, and metric-optimized molecule synthesis, but efforts to solve these problems using machine learning have also increased in recent years. In this work, we propose the use of attention to study functional groups and other property-impacting molecular substructures from a data-driven perspective, using a transformer-based model (BERT) on datasets of string representations of molecules and analyzing the behavior of its attention heads. We then apply the representations of functional groups and atoms learned by the model to tackle problems of toxicity, solubility, drug-likeness, and synthesis accessibility on smaller datasets using the learned representations as features for graph convolution and attention models on the graph structure of molecules, as well as fine-tuning of BERT. Finally, we propose the use of attention visualization as a helpful tool for chemistry practitioners and students to quickly identify important substructures in various chemical properties.

papers.title: Resurrecting the Salmon: Rethinking Mechanistic Interpretability with Domain-Specific Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improve reconstruction fidelity and interpretability compared to broad-domain SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improves reconstruction fidelity, interpretability, and reduces linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggests the field may need to question 'foundation-model' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Domain-specific SAEs achieve 15-20% higher fraction of variance explained and better loss recovery than broad-domain SAEs.
Domain-specific SAEs produce features that are more interpretable and aligned with clinically meaningful concepts.
Domain-specific SAEs capture more linear structure, leaving a smaller and more nonlinear residual error (less dark matter).
Domain-specific SAEs show improved cosine similarity between activations and reconstructions.
Domain-specific SAEs have minimal shrinkage (relative reconstruction bias close to 1).
future_direction: Extending domain-specific SAEs to other specialised domains, such as legal or financial text.
Investigating how domain confinement affects feature splitting and absorption.
Studying the trade-offs between domain breadth and SAE performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose large language model (LLM) activations into latent features that reveal mechanistic structure. Conventional SAEs train on broad data distributions, forcing a fixed latent budget to capture only high-frequency, generic patterns. This often results in significant linear ``dark matter'' in reconstruction error and produces latents that fragment or absorb each other, complicating interpretation. We show that restricting SAE training to a well-defined domain (medical text) reallocates capacity to domain-specific features, improving both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability. Training JumpReLU SAEs on layer-20 activations of Gemma-2 models using 195k clinical QA examples, we find that domain-confined SAEs explain up to 20\% more variance, achieve higher loss recovery, and reduce linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs. Automated and human evaluations confirm that learned features align with clinically meaningful concepts (e.g., ``taste sensations'' or ``infectious mononucleosis''), rather than frequent but uninformative tokens. These domain-specific SAEs capture relevant linear structure, leaving a smaller, more purely nonlinear residual. We conclude that domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggesting the field may need to question ``foundation-model'' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.

papers.title: Probing Graph Representations
papers.research_question: What is encoded in the representations learned by graph-based models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a probing framework to analyze graph representations and shows that transformer-based graph models capture more chemically relevant information compared to message-passing GNNs.
papers.conclusion: Probing is a useful diagnostic tool for understanding and evaluating graph-based models, especially in capturing domain-relevant information.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer-based models capture more chemically relevant information in their representations.
Randomly initialized models can also encode useful features, sometimes on par with pretrained models.
Skip connections help preserve information across layers.
Pairwise probing can isolate the effect of specific properties and show causal relationships.
papers.abstract: Today we have a good theoretical understanding of the representational power of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). For example, their limitations have been characterized in relation to a hierarchy of Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) isomorphism tests. However, we do not know what is encoded in the learned representations. This is our main question. We answer it using a probing framework to quantify the amount of meaningful information captured in graph representations. Our findings on molecular datasets show the potential of probing for understanding the inductive biases of graph-based models. We compare different families of models and show that transformer-based models capture more chemically relevant information compared to models based on message passing. We also study the effect of different design choices such as skip connections and virtual nodes. We advocate for probing as a useful diagnostic tool for evaluating graph-based models.

papers.title: Decomposing Representation Space into Interpretable Subspaces with Unsupervised Learning
papers.research_question: Can we find interpretable subspaces in neural representations in an unsupervised way? To what extent are different aspects organized in separate subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (NDM) to decompose representation space into interpretable subspaces, showing that these subspaces align with known circuit variables and can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Unsupervised decomposition of representation space into interpretable subspaces is possible, and these subspaces can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis, offering a new perspective on understanding model internals.
papers.key_findings:
NDM can find interpretable subspaces without supervision, as shown in toy models and real language models.
Subspaces found by NDM align with variables in known circuits in GPT-2, as evidenced by high Gini coefficients in subspace patching experiments.
The method scales to 2B models, finding separate subspaces for context and parametric knowledge routing.
Qualitative analysis shows that subspaces are consistent and interpretable across different inputs.
papers.limitation: The method can get stuck in local minima, leading to sub-optimal subspace partitions.
future_direction: hierarchical structure of subspaces
more flexible searching over dimension configurations
applying the method to larger models and more tasks
papers.abstract: Understanding internal representations of neural models is a core interest of mechanistic interpretability. Due to its large dimensionality, the representation space can encode various aspects about inputs. To what extent are different aspects organized and encoded in separate subspaces? Is it possible to find these ``natural'' subspaces in a purely unsupervised way? Somewhat surprisingly, we can indeed achieve this and find interpretable subspaces by a seemingly unrelated training objective. Our method, neighbor distance minimization (NDM), learns non-basis-aligned subspaces in an unsupervised manner. Qualitative analysis shows subspaces are interpretable in many cases, and encoded information in obtained subspaces tends to share the same abstract concept across different inputs, making such subspaces similar to ``variables'' used by the model. We also conduct quantitative experiments using known circuits in GPT-2; results show a strong connection between subspaces and circuit variables. We also provide evidence showing scalability to 2B models by finding separate subspaces mediating context and parametric knowledge routing. Viewed more broadly, our findings offer a new perspective on understanding model internals and building circuits.

papers.title: LLaVA Steering: Visual Instruction Tuning with 500x Fewer Parameters through Modality Linear Representation-Steering
papers.research_question: How can the number of trainable parameters for visual instruction tuning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be significantly reduced by addressing the intrinsic imbalance between text and visual modalities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Modality Linear Representation-Steering (MoReS), a method that rebalances text and visual modalities in MLLMs by steering visual representations through linear transformations, achieving comparable performance to LoRA with 500x fewer trainable parameters.
papers.conclusion: MoReS provides an efficient and effective approach for visual instruction tuning in MLLMs by addressing modality imbalance, significantly reducing parameter count while maintaining performance, and offering a pathway for more accessible and customizable multimodal model development.
papers.key_findings:
MoReS requires 287 to 1,150 times fewer trainable parameters than LoRA while maintaining competitive performance on multiple visual benchmarks.
MoReS effectively rebalances the attention distribution between visual and textual representations, mitigating the intrinsic modality imbalance in MLLMs.
The method reduces hallucination in MLLMs, as shown by improved performance on POPE and HallucinationBench.
MoReS preserves the LLM's pre-trained world knowledge and performs well on text-only tasks, demonstrating its generalizability.
A dynamic steering ratio mechanism allows MoReS to adapt to tasks of varying complexity, with optimal ratios differing per dataset.
papers.abstract: Jinhe Bi, Yujun Wang, Haokun Chen, Xun Xiao, Artur Hecker, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Attention network for predicting T-cell receptor–peptide binding can associate attention with interpretable protein structural properties
papers.research_question: Can an attention-based neural network accurately predict TCR-pMHC interactions and provide interpretable biological insights into TCR function and CDR3-peptide binding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a cross-attention based model (cross-TCR-interpreter) for predicting TCR-peptide binding, which achieves competitive performance and provides interpretable insights by associating attention weights with protein structural properties such as hydrogen bonds.
papers.conclusion: The study presents a computational approach for predicting TCR binding to specific ligand peptides using a cross-attention mechanism, and by analyzing protein structures, it gains new insights into TCR-peptide functional relationships.
papers.key_findings:
The cross-TCR-interpreter model achieves competitive performance on benchmark datasets for TCR-peptide binding prediction.
The model's attention weights can be statistically associated with structural properties, showing that largely attended residues are more likely to form hydrogen bonds within CDR3s.
The model struggles to generalize to unseen peptides, as evidenced by poor performance on the COVID-19 dataset and recent data test set.
Input perturbation analysis shows that altering attended residues can significantly change predictions, indicating the importance of these residues.
The attention mechanism provides interpretable insights into the binding mechanism, suggesting that internal hydrogen bonds within CDR3s may stabilize binding conformations.
papers.limitation:
The model's performance on unseen peptides is poor, as shown in the COVID-19 dataset and recent data test set.
The simplified focus on CDR3 regions might miss integral information from the complete TCR and MHC, potentially overlooking critical interactions.
The interpretability of attention values might be influenced by the imbalance in the dataset, with more TCR samples than peptide samples.
future_direction: Using different machine learning models such as meaningful perturbation methods on exhaustively collected sequences.
Incorporating more comprehensive methods like molecular simulations for a fuller view of the binding mechanism.
Improving generalization to unseen peptides by addressing dataset limitations.
papers.abstract: Understanding how a T-cell receptor (TCR) recognizes its specific ligand peptide is crucial for gaining an insight into biological functions and disease mechanisms. Despite its importance, experimentally determining TCR-peptide-major histocompatibility complex (TCR-pMHC) interactions is expensive and time-consuming. To address this challenge, computational methods have been proposed, but they are typically evaluated by internal retrospective validation only, and few researchers have incorporated and tested an attention layer from language models into structural information. Therefore, in this study, we developed a machine learning model based on a modified version of Transformer, a source-target attention neural network, to predict the TCR-pMHC interaction solely from the amino acid sequences of the TCR complementarity-determining region (CDR) 3 and the peptide. This model achieved competitive performance on a benchmark dataset of the TCR-pMHC interaction, as well as on a truly new external dataset. Additionally, by analyzing the results of binding predictions, we associated the neural network weights with protein structural properties. By classifying the residues into large- and small-attention groups, we identified statistically significant properties associated with the largely attended residues such as hydrogen bonds within CDR3. The dataset that we created and the ability of our model to provide an interpretable prediction of TCR-peptide binding should increase our knowledge about molecular recognition and pave the way for designing new therapeutics.

papers.title: Explainability Techniques for Chemical Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we explain the predictions of chemical language models by attributing importance to individual atoms in the input molecular string?
papers.core_contribution: We propose an explainable AI technique for chemical language models that attributes the importance of individual atoms to the model's predictions by backpropagating relevance through attention scores and gradients, and visualize the importance on the molecular structure.
papers.conclusion: We propose an attribution technique for Transformers operating on molecular string representations, which provides interpretable predictions and allows inspection of the model's learned features for solubility prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method achieves competitive predictive performance on aqueous and organic solvent solubility prediction tasks.
The visualizations highlight atoms that are important for solubility, which can be validated by chemists.
The model sometimes attributes high relevance to the carbon backbone, which may be due to the pretraining procedure.
The method is applicable to self-attention Transformers and can be extended to other architectures.
papers.limitation:
The method only visualizes atom tokens and does not handle non-atom tokens (e.g., bonds, brackets) in the SMILES string.
The model does not enforce invariance to different SMILES representations of the same molecule.
future_direction: Extend the visualization to non-atom tokens in the SMILES string.
Enforce SMILES invariance in the model through contrastive training.
Apply the explainability technique to other Transformer architectures, such as generative models.
papers.abstract: Explainability techniques are crucial in gaining insights into the reasons behind the predictions of deep learning models, which have not yet been applied to chemical language models. We propose an explainable AI technique that attributes the importance of individual atoms towards the predictions made by these models. Our method backpropagates the relevance information towards the chemical input string and visualizes the importance of individual atoms. We focus on self-attention Transformers operating on molecular string representations and leverage a pretrained encoder for finetuning. We showcase the method by predicting and visualizing solubility in water and organic solvents. We achieve competitive model performance while obtaining interpretable predictions, which we use to inspect the pretrained model.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Network Models for Toxicity Prediction by Extracting Learned Chemical Features
papers.research_question: How can neural network models for toxicity prediction be interpreted by extracting learned chemical features from hidden layers?
papers.core_contribution: A novel method to interpret neural network predictions for toxicity by extracting chemical substructures from hidden neurons, validated on mutagenicity data and shown to be competitive with established attribution methods.
papers.conclusion: The study presents a novel method to extract learned chemical information from hidden layers of neural networks and use these to explain model predictions, complementing more established techniques for understanding neural network models for toxicity prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The activation of hidden neurons in a neural network trained for toxicity prediction can be linked to specific chemical substructures (toxicophores).
The proposed method can extract substructures that correspond to known toxicophores for mutagenicity.
The explanations provided by the method (IG_hidden) are competitive with and complementary to those from input feature attribution (IG_input).
The method works well for single-layer networks but for deeper layers, neurons tend to aggregate multiple features and become less specific.
papers.limitation:
One neuron may be activated by a range of diverse chemical substructures, making it impossible to assign a single cause to the activation of a particular neuron.
Relevant chemical features may activate a large number of different neurons across the network, making interpretation complex.
It could be that none of the identified substructures associated with a highly activated neuron match the test compound.
future_direction: Extending the approach to regression models.
Using more generic representations of substructures such as SMARTS.
Applying the method to other toxicity endpoints and datasets.
papers.abstract: Neural network models have become a popular machine-learning technique for the toxicity prediction of chemicals. However, due to their complex structure, it is difficult to understand predictions made by these models which limits confidence. Current techniques to tackle this problem such as SHAP or integrated gradients provide insights by attributing importance to the input features of individual compounds. While these methods have produced promising results in some cases, they do not shed light on how representations of compounds are transformed in hidden layers, which constitute how neural networks learn. We present a novel technique to interpret neural networks which identifies chemical substructures in training data found to be responsible for the activation of hidden neurons. For individual test compounds, the importance of hidden neurons is determined, and the associated substructures are leveraged to explain the model prediction. Using structural alerts for mutagenicity from the Derek Nexus expert system as ground truth, we demonstrate the validity of the approach and show that model explanations are competitive with and complementary to explanations obtained from an established feature attribution method.

papers.title: Structure and Representation in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we find modular structure in neural networks, and does this structure have functional relevance in terms of local specialization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that trained neural networks exhibit clusterability (modular structure) and that clustering can find locally specialized groups of neurons. It also shows that interpretability tools reveal shortcomings in reward models' feature representation and generalization.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation advances understanding of neural network structure and representation, and highlights the need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Trained neural networks are more clusterable than randomly initialized networks.
Clustering finds groups of neurons that are important and coherent, indicating local specialization.
Interpretability tools applied to reward models show they do not adequately represent relevant features and mispredict reward out of distribution.
These tools do not reveal a clear picture of the computation the networks are performing.
There is a need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behavior.
papers.limitation: Interpretability tools do not reveal a clear picture of what computation the networks are performing.
future_direction: Applying the methods to larger networks.
Studying the dynamics of clusterability during training.
Developing better interpretability tools for understanding generalization.
papers.abstract: Since neural networks have become dominant within the field of artificial intelligence, a sub-field of research has emerged attempting to understand their inner workings. One standard method within this sub-field has been to primarily understand neural networks as representing human-comprehensible features. Another possibility that has been less explored is to understand them as multi-step computer programs. A seeming prerequisite for this is some form of modularity: for different parts of the network to operate independently enough to be understood in isolation, and to implement distinct interpretable sub-routines.To find modular structure inside neural networks, we initially use the tools of graphical clustering. A network is clusterable in this sense if it can be divided into groups of neurons with strong internal connectivity but weak external connectivity. We find that a trained neural network is typically more clusterable than randomly initialized networks, and often clusterable relative to random networks with the same distribution of weights as the trained network. We investigate factors that promote clusterability, and also develop novel methods targeted at that end.For modularity to be valuable for understanding neural networks, it needs to have some sort of functional relevance.The type of functional relevance we target is local specialization of functionality. A neural network is locally specialized to the extent that parts of its computational graph can be abstractly represented as performing some comprehensible sub-task relevant to the overall task. We propose two proxies for local specialization: importance, which reflects how valuable sets of neurons are to network performance; and coherence, which reflects how consistently their neurons associate with features of the inputs. We then operationalize these proxies using techniques conventionally used to interpret individual neurons, applying them instead to groups of neurons produced by graph clustering algorithms. Our results show that clustering succeeds at finding groups of neurons that are important and coherent, although not all groups of neurons found are so.We conclude with a case study of using more standard interpretability tools, designed to understand the features being represented by directions in activation space, applying them to the analysis of neural networks trained on the reward function of the game CoinRun. Despite our networks achieving a low test loss, the application of interpretability tools shows that networks do not adequately represent relevant features and badly mispredict reward out of distribution. That said, these tools do not reveal a clear picture of what computation the networks are in fact performing. This not only illustrates the need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behaviour, but motivates it: if we take these networks as models of 'motivation systems' of policies trained by reinforcement learning, the conclusion is that such networks may competently pursue the wrong objectives when deployed in richer environments, indicating a need for interpretability techniques to shed light on generalization behaviour.

papers.title: Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning in Transformers work? The paper hypothesizes that Transformers implement gradient descent in their forward pass to learn from in-context data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformers trained on auto-regressive objectives implement gradient descent in their forward pass, providing a mechanistic understanding of in-context learning for regression tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning in Transformers can be understood as gradient descent in the forward pass, at least for regression tasks, providing a mechanistic understanding.
papers.key_findings:
A single linear self-attention layer can be constructed to perform one step of gradient descent on a linear regression loss.
When trained on linear regression tasks, linear self-attention-only Transformers converge to weights that match the gradient descent construction.
Multiple layers of self-attention can implement multiple steps of gradient descent and even surpass plain gradient descent by learning a curvature correction (GD++).
Transformers with MLPs can solve nonlinear regression tasks by learning linear models on deep representations.
The paper connects the induction head mechanism to in-context learning by gradient descent.
papers.limitation:
The findings on linear self-attention-only Transformers only explain a limited part of a complex process, and it may be one of many possible methods giving rise to in-context learning.
The analysis is limited to regression tasks and simple Transformer architectures.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to language modeling and other domains.
Investigating the role of softmax and LayerNorm in in-context learning.
Exploring the connection to hypernetworks and weight generation.
papers.abstract: At present, the mechanisms of in-context learning in Transformers are not well understood and remain mostly an intuition. In this paper, we suggest that training Transformers on auto-regressive objectives is closely related to gradient-based meta-learning formulations. We start by providing a simple weight construction that shows the equivalence of data transformations induced by 1) a single linear self-attention layer and by 2) gradient-descent (GD) on a regression loss. Motivated by that construction, we show empirically that when training self-attention-only Transformers on simple regression tasks either the models learned by GD and Transformers show great similarity or, remarkably, the weights found by optimization match the construction. Thus we show how trained Transformers become mesa-optimizers i.e. learn models by gradient descent in their forward pass. This allows us, at least in the domain of regression problems, to mechanistically understand the inner workings of in-context learning in optimized Transformers. Building on this insight, we furthermore identify how Transformers surpass the performance of plain gradient descent by learning an iterative curvature correction and learn linear models on deep data representations to solve non-linear regression tasks. Finally, we discuss intriguing parallels to a mechanism identified to be crucial for in-context learning termed induction-head (Olsson et al., 2022) and show how it could be understood as a specific case of in-context learning by gradient descent learning within Transformers. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at https://github.com/google-research/self-organising-systems/tree/master/transformers_learn_icl_by_gd .

papers.title: Exploring the LLM Journey from Cognition to Expression with Linear Representations
papers.research_question: How do cognitive and expressive capabilities develop and interact in large language models across pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback stages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cognitive capabilities in LLMs are established during pretraining, while expressive capabilities develop during SFT and RLHF, with cognitive capability setting an upper bound for expressive capability.
papers.conclusion: This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of LLM training processes.
papers.key_findings:
Cognitive capability is primarily established during the pretraining stage, whereas expressive capability develops during SFT and RLHF.
There is a strong statistical correlation between cognitive and expressive capabilities, with cognitive capability acting as an upper bound.
The gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities can be bridged by optimization-free methods such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling.
The vocabulary linear layer plays a crucial role in expressive capability, and its training during SFT/RLHF helps reduce the gap.
Layer-wise analysis reveals a plateau in cognitive capability in deeper layers, indicating redundancy in the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring additional linear analysis techniques for model analysis and control.
papers.abstract: This paper presents an in-depth examination of the evolution and interplay of cognitive and expressive capabilities in large language models (LLMs), with a specific focus on Baichuan-7B and Baichuan-33B, an advanced bilingual (Chinese and English) LLM series. We define and explore the model's cognitive and expressive capabilities through linear representations across three critical phases: Pretraining, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Cognitive capability is defined as the quantity and quality of information conveyed by the neuron output vectors within the network, similar to the neural signal processing in human cognition. Expressive capability is defined as the model's capability to produce word-level output. Our findings unveil a sequential development pattern, where cognitive abilities are largely established during Pretraining, whereas expressive abilities predominantly advance during SFT and RLHF. Statistical analyses confirm a significant correlation between the two capabilities, suggesting that cognitive capacity may limit expressive potential. The paper also explores the theoretical underpinnings of these divergent developmental trajectories and their connection to the LLMs' architectural design. Moreover, we evaluate various optimization-independent strategies, such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling, which bridge the gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities. This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of their training processes.

papers.title: Superior Molecular Representations from Intermediate Encoder Layers
papers.research_question: Are we overlooking superior molecular representations by adhering to the final-layer convention in chemistry? Specifically, do intermediate layers of molecular encoders provide more informative and task-relevant features for downstream property prediction than the final layer?
papers.core_contribution: Intermediate layers of pretrained molecular encoders retain more general-purpose features and yield superior performance on downstream property prediction tasks compared to the final layer, both when used as frozen embeddings and when finetuned, leading to substantial performance improvements and computational efficiency.
papers.conclusion: The common practice of relying solely on final-layer representations from pretrained molecular encoders is suboptimal; exploring intermediate layers yields substantial performance gains and computational savings, advocating for a shift beyond the final-layer default.
papers.key_findings:
Using frozen embeddings from optimal intermediate layers improves downstream performance by an average of 5.4% (up to 28.6%) compared to the final-layer, with 81% of model-task combinations preferring a non-final layer.
Finetuning encoders truncated at intermediate depths achieves average improvements of 8.5% (up to 40.8%) over finetuning the complete encoder, with 71% of cases showing gains.
Label-free probes (tokenized-molecule entropy and adjacent-layer CKA) show that final layers undergo specialization and compression, while intermediate layers retain more transferable features.
The optimal intermediate layer varies by encoder architecture and downstream task; no single depth is universally best.
Frozen embedding performance correlates with finetuning performance (median Pearson correlation 0.60), providing an efficient proxy for selecting layers to finetune.
papers.limitation: The study is constrained by computational resources to five encoders and 22 ADMET tasks; extending the analysis to a broader set of molecular encoders and chemical domains could further validate the findings.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to a broader set of molecular encoders and chemical domains.
Conduct future work with additional architectures, multiple random seeds, and more exhaustive hyperparameter searches for deeper insights and more robust generalizations.
papers.abstract: Pretrained molecular encoders have become indispensable in computational chemistry for tasks such as property prediction and molecular generation. However, the standard practice of relying solely on final-layer embeddings for downstream tasks may discard valuable information. In this work, we first analyze the information flow in five diverse molecular encoders and find that intermediate layers retain more general-purpose features, whereas the final-layer specializes and compresses information. We then perform an empirical layer-wise evaluation across 22 property prediction tasks. We find that using frozen embeddings from optimal intermediate layers improves downstream performance by an average of 5.4%, up to 28.6%, compared to the final-layer. Furthermore, finetuning encoders truncated at intermediate depths achieves even greater average improvements of 8.5%, with increases as high as 40.8%, obtaining new state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. These findings highlight the importance of exploring the full representational depth of molecular encoders to achieve substantial performance improvements and computational efficiency. The code will be made publicly available.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: An Analysis of Encoder Representations in Transformer-Based Machine Translation
papers.research_question: What kind of linguistic information (syntactic and semantic) is learned by the encoder of Transformer-based machine translation models, and how does it vary across layers and models with different translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes encoder representations in Transformer-based machine translation and finds that specific attention heads capture syntactic dependencies, with lower layers encoding more syntax and higher layers more semantics.
papers.conclusion: The experimental evaluation sheds light on interesting findings about dependency relations and syntactic and semantic behavior across layers in Transformer encoder representations.
papers.key_findings:
Each layer has at least one attention head that encodes a significant amount of syntactic dependencies.
Lower layers tend to encode more syntactic information, while upper layers move towards semantic tasks.
The information about the length of the input sentence starts to vanish after the third layer.
Attention can be used to transfer knowledge between high- and low-resource languages, improving translation quality.
future_direction: Extend the analysis with probing tasks to evaluate other linguistic properties.
Use a recent evaluation dataset for analysis.
Analyze the attention weights between the encoder and the decoder.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is a successful technique in modern NLP, especially in tasks like machine translation. The recently proposed network architecture of the Transformer is based entirely on attention mechanisms and achieves new state of the art results in neural machine translation, outperforming other sequence-to-sequence models. However, so far not much is known about the internal properties of the model and the representations it learns to achieve that performance. To study this question, we investigate the information that is learned by the attention mechanism in Transformer models with different translation quality. We assess the representations of the encoder by extracting dependency relations based on self-attention weights, we perform four probing tasks to study the amount of syntactic and semantic captured information and we also test attention in a transfer learning scenario. Our analysis sheds light on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the various encoder representations. We observe that specific attention heads mark syntactic dependency relations and we can also confirm that lower layers tend to learn more about syntax while higher layers tend to encode more semantics.

papers.title: Rethinking LLM-as-a-Judge: Representation-as-a-Judge with Small Language Models via Semantic Capacity Asymmetry
papers.research_question: Can small language models serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations, even when their generation is poor?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis and introduces INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that extracts evaluation signals from small model representations, enabling efficient and accurate reference-free evaluation.
papers.conclusion: Small LMs retain strong evaluative signals in their internal representations, and the Representation-as-a-Judge paradigm via INSPECTOR offers a scalable and interpretable solution for evaluation and data curation.
papers.key_findings:
Small LMs encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states despite weak generation.
Probing internal representations with INSPECTOR outperforms prompt-based evaluation with small LMs and closely approximates large LLM judges.
The Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis is supported: evaluation requires less semantic capacity than generation.
Probing classifiers can serve as reliable data filters for supervised fine-tuning, leading to performance gains.
Larger LLMs do not necessarily provide stronger evaluation signals than smaller ones.
papers.limitation:
Multiclass prediction performance of probing classifiers is modest (50-60%) compared to binary classification.
Out-of-distribution generalization for multiclass probing is limited, with F1 scores dropping significantly.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as reference-free evaluators via prompting, but this "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm is costly, opaque, and sensitive to prompt design. In this work, we investigate whether smaller models can serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations instead of surface generation. We uncover a consistent empirical pattern: small LMs, despite with weak generative ability, encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states. This motivates us to propose the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis: evaluation requires significantly less semantic capacity than generation and can be grounded in intermediate representations, suggesting that evaluation does not necessarily need to rely on large-scale generative models but can instead leverage latent features from smaller ones. Our findings motivate a paradigm shift from LLM-as-a-Judge to Representation-as-a-Judge, a decoding-free evaluation strategy that probes internal model structure rather than relying on prompted output. We instantiate this paradigm through INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that predicts aspect-level evaluation scores from small model representations. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, GPQA) show that INSPECTOR substantially outperforms prompting-based small LMs and closely approximates full LLM judges, while offering a more efficient, reliable, and interpretable alternative for scalable evaluation.

papers.title: Improving Neuron-level Interpretability with White-box Language Models
papers.research_question: Can building sparsity directly into the language model architecture (via a white-box design) improve neuron-level interpretability compared to post-hoc methods like sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a white-box transformer-like architecture (crate) that embeds sparse coding directly into the model, leading to significantly improved neuron-level interpretability compared to standard transformers like GPT-2.
papers.conclusion: Replacing the standard transformer architecture with the white-box crate model significantly improves neuron-level interpretability, pointing towards a promising direction for building more interpretable foundation models with built-in sparse coding.
papers.key_findings:
crate achieves up to 103% relative improvement in neuron-level interpretability over GPT-2 across multiple evaluation metrics.
The improved interpretability is steady across different layers and model sizes.
crate's interpretability stems from its ability to consistently and distinctively activate on relevant tokens.
crate has more optimal representations for interpretability than GPT-2, as applying sparse autoencoders (SAE) to crate yields smaller improvements than applying SAE to GPT-2.
crate can be steered without the reconstruction loss inherent in post-hoc SAE methods.
papers.limitation: The performance of crate on the next-token prediction task is not as good as GPT-2, potentially due to the introduction of sparsity.
future_direction: Investigate a better trade-off between performance and interpretability in language models with built-in sparsity.
Research more qualitative mechanisms in white-box language models and how to use them for downstream edits.
papers.abstract: Neurons in auto-regressive language models like GPT-2 can be interpreted by analyzing their activation patterns. Recent studies have shown that techniques such as dictionary learning, a form of post-hoc sparse coding, enhance this neuron-level interpretability. In our research, we are driven by the goal to fundamentally improve neural network interpretability by embedding sparse coding directly within the model architecture, rather than applying it as an afterthought. In our study, we introduce a white-box transformer-like architecture named Coding RAte TransformEr (CRATE), explicitly engineered to capture sparse, low-dimensional structures within data distributions. Our comprehensive experiments showcase significant improvements (up to 103% relative improvement) in neuron-level interpretability across a variety of evaluation metrics. Detailed investigations confirm that this enhanced interpretability is steady across different layers irrespective of the model size, underlining CRATE's robust performance in enhancing neural network interpretability. Further analysis shows that CRATE's increased interpretability comes from its enhanced ability to consistently and distinctively activate on relevant tokens. These findings point towards a promising direction for creating white-box foundation models that excel in neuron-level interpretation.

papers.title: Disentangling Neuron Representations with Concept Vectors
papers.research_question: How can we find meaningful directions (concept vectors) in activation space that correspond to distinct features, starting from polysemantic neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into concept vectors that represent distinct features, allowing for fine-grained concept separation controlled by a distance threshold.
papers.conclusion: Exploring directions in activation space (concept vectors) instead of individual neurons can lead to finding coherent fundamental units, bridging mechanistic interpretability and concept discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic neurons can be disentangled into concept vectors that are linear combinations of neurons.
The concept vectors encode coherent, human-understandable features, as validated by human experiments.
The method can separate fine-grained concepts (e.g., underwater scenes vs. scuba divers) by adjusting a distance threshold.
The latent space representations have higher similarity with the discovered concept vectors than with the neuron directions.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the data used to generate clusters.
All experiments were performed on image data, which may limit generalizability to other data types.
future_direction: Generalizing the method to other data types such as language and tabular data.
Looking at other starting candidates for concepts besides neurons.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand how models store representations by breaking down neural networks into interpretable units. However, the occurrence of polysemantic neurons, or neurons that respond to multiple unrelated features, makes interpreting individual neurons challenging. This has led to the search for meaningful vectors, known as concept vectors, in activation space instead of individual neurons. The main contribution of this paper is a method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into concept vectors encapsulating distinct features. Our method can search for fine-grained concepts according to the user’s desired level of concept separation. The analysis shows that polysemantic neurons can be disentangled into directions consisting of linear combinations of neurons. Our evaluations show that the concept vectors found encode coherent, human-understandable features.

papers.title: Diverging views on the role of structured representations in linguistics and language modeling
papers.research_question: How do language models compare to human language processing in terms of structured representations, and what is their role in the science of language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that language models struggle with structured representations central to human language, and suggests that for language models to be effective models of language, structured representations must be incorporated as computational objects.
papers.conclusion: Language models need to conceptualize structured representations as computational objects to better align with human language and contribute to the science of language.
papers.key_findings:
Language models trained on next-word prediction may not learn structure-dependent representations necessary for human language.
Models like ChatGPT show insensitivity to Binding Principle C, incorrectly allowing co-reference in prohibited contexts.
Language models do not make a qualitative distinction between possible and impossible languages, treating them similarly unlike humans.
The internal representational infrastructure for possible and impossible languages overlaps in models, indicating no fundamental difference.
Incorporating structured representations as primary computational targets could enhance language models' utility as models of language.
future_direction: Incorporate structured representations as computational objects in language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent years have seen dramatic advances in the linguistic abilities of language models, leading some authors to argue that they can be treated as models of language. Against this background, we provide a cognitive perspective on the place of language models in the science of language, with a particular focus on the role of structured representations. Evidence from linguistics, psychology and cognitive neuroscience shows that structured representations occupy a central place in the human mind. Structured representations constrain how linguistic forms map onto meanings, thereby determining the boundaries of possible human languages. In language modeling, instead, the place of structured representations is often peripheral. They are seen as optional end point of modeling, to be induced as a consequence of the objective the model tries to optimize – that is, next-word prediction. Because structured relations and representations are not necessarily useful for predicting the next word in a sequence, it is not guaranteed that the model’s internal organization will come to encode those representations. Indeed, contemporary language models struggle to use structured representations functionally to map form onto meaning, and to determine whether they should consider their input as a possible human language or not. Building on classic insights in linguistics and (computational) cognitive science, we suggest that any use of language models as models of language requires conceptualizing the role of structured representations as computational objects.

papers.title: Structural Persistence in Language Models: Priming as a Window into Abstract Language Representations
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether modern neural language models exhibit structural priming, what factors influence the priming effect, and the nature of the structural representations they acquire.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer language models exhibit structural priming, indicating they encode abstract structural information, and that this priming is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, with evidence for hierarchical syntactic representations.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that Transformer language models are susceptible to structural priming, revealing they encode abstract structural information that is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, and may involve hierarchical syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer language models show evidence of structural priming.
Priming strength is boosted by semantic similarity and lexical overlap between prime and target sentences.
Priming effects persist but are asymmetrical when primes are semantically implausible.
Priming strength increases with recency (proximity) and cumulative exposure to the prime structure.
The structural representations may encode hierarchical syntactic information, as shown by priming with nested dependencies.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on only two syntactic alternations in English.
The corpus is template-based and may not capture naturalistic language.
Only auto-regressive language models are considered; masked LMs are not investigated.
future_direction: Extend the investigation to other syntactic constructions and languages.
Use more naturalistic data beyond template-based corpora.
Investigate structural priming in masked language models.
papers.abstract: Abstract We investigate the extent to which modern neural language models are susceptible to structural priming, the phenomenon whereby the structure of a sentence makes the same structure more probable in a follow-up sentence. We explore how priming can be used to study the potential of these models to learn abstract structural information, which is a prerequisite for good performance on tasks that require natural language understanding skills. We introduce a novel metric and release Prime-LM, a large corpus where we control for various linguistic factors that interact with priming strength. We find that Transformer models indeed show evidence of structural priming, but also that the generalizations they learned are to some extent modulated by semantic information. Our experiments also show that the representations acquired by the models may not only encode abstract sequential structure but involve certain level of hierarchical syntactic information. More generally, our study shows that the priming paradigm is a useful, additional tool for gaining insights into the capacities of language models and opens the door to future priming-based investigations that probe the model’s internal states.1

papers.title: Revisiting In-context Learning Inference Circuit in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the inference circuit that explains the observed phenomena of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a comprehensive 3-step inference circuit (input text encode, semantics merge, feature retrieval and copy) to characterize the inference dynamics of in-context learning in large language models, and provides empirical evidence that it captures many observed ICL phenomena and is a dominant mechanism.
papers.conclusion: The proposed 3-step inference circuit successfully captures and unifies many fragmented phenomena observed during in-context learning, providing a comprehensive and practical explanation of ICL inference in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Large language models encode input text into linear, task-relevant representations in the hidden states of forerunner tokens, and this encoding is enhanced by demonstrations.
Forerunner token heads copy text representations into label tokens without selectivity, forming joint representations of label semantics and text features.
Induction heads retrieve label representations similar to the query in task-specific subspaces and copy them to the query, enabling ICL prediction.
The proposed circuit explains phenomena such as positional bias, noise robustness, and demonstration saturation in ICL.
Ablation analysis shows the circuit is a dominant mechanism for ICL, but bypass mechanisms exist in parallel.
papers.limitation: The proposed circuit may not generalize to in-weight learning (IWL) scenarios, where the query's ground-truth label is not present in the demonstrations.
future_direction: Exploring different inference dynamics in in-weight learning (IWL) scenarios.
papers.abstract: In-context Learning (ICL) is an emerging few-shot learning paradigm on Language Models (LMs) with inner mechanisms un-explored. There are already existing works describing the inner processing of ICL, while they struggle to capture all the inference phenomena in large language models. Therefore, this paper proposes a comprehensive circuit to model the inference dynamics and try to explain the observed phenomena of ICL. In detail, we divide ICL inference into 3 major operations: (1) Input Text Encode: LMs encode every input text (in the demonstrations and queries) into linear representation in the hidden states with sufficient information to solve ICL tasks. (2) Semantics Merge: LMs merge the encoded representations of demonstrations with their corresponding label tokens to produce joint representations of labels and demonstrations. (3) Feature Retrieval and Copy: LMs search the joint representations of demonstrations similar to the query representation on a task subspace, and copy the searched representations into the query. Then, language model heads capture these copied label representations to a certain extent and decode them into predicted labels. Through careful measurements, the proposed inference circuit successfully captures and unifies many fragmented phenomena observed during the ICL process, making it a comprehensive and practical explanation of the ICL inference process. Moreover, ablation analysis by disabling the proposed steps seriously damages the ICL performance, suggesting the proposed inference circuit is a dominating mechanism. Additionally, we confirm and list some bypass mechanisms that solve ICL tasks in parallel with the proposed circuit.

papers.title: Towards Uncovering How Large Language Model Works: An Explainability Perspective
papers.research_question: How can explainability techniques uncover the internal mechanisms of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: This survey paper provides a systematic overview of existing explainability techniques, including mechanistic interpretability and representation engineering, to uncover the inner workings of large language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that explainability techniques like mechanistic interpretability and representation engineering are crucial for understanding LLMs, but there are still challenges such as scalability and evaluation of explanations.
papers.limitation: The survey does not explore the complete landscape of relevant XAI methods for understanding LLMs, due to space constraints.
future_direction: Developing scalable techniques to analyze and interpret the intricate knowledge structures embedded within LLMs.
Revealing the intricate mechanisms that give rise to advanced reasoning capabilities in LLMs.
Fully leveraging insights from explainability to develop techniques that can substantially improve LLM performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have led to breakthroughs in language tasks, yet the internal mechanisms that enable their remarkable generalization and reasoning abilities remain opaque. This lack of transparency presents challenges such as hallucinations, toxicity, and misalignment with human values, hindering the safe and beneficial deployment of LLMs. This paper aims to uncover the mechanisms underlying LLM functionality through the lens of explainability. First, we review how knowledge is architecturally composed within LLMs and encoded in their internal parameters via mechanistic interpretability techniques. Then, we summarize how knowledge is embedded in LLM representations by leveraging probing techniques and representation engineering. Additionally, we investigate the training dynamics through a mechanistic perspective to explain phenomena such as grokking and memorization. Lastly, we explore how the insights gained from these explanations can enhance LLM performance through model editing, improve efficiency through pruning, and better align with human values.

papers.title: Beyond Interpretability: The Gains of Feature Monosemanticity on Model Robustness
papers.research_question: Does feature monosemanticity, which improves interpretability, also improve model robustness, challenging the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff?
papers.core_contribution: This paper challenges the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff by showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also provide concrete gains in model robustness across various scenarios including noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that monosemanticity offers advantages beyond interpretability, improving model robustness across multiple learning scenarios, and advocates for exploring its broader learning benefits.
papers.key_findings:
Monosemantic features (from NCL or SAE) are more robust than polysemantic features under linear probing with label noise and input noise.
Maintaining monosemanticity during finetuning (via non-negative tuning) reduces overfitting and improves performance in few-shot and noisy-label settings.
MonoLoRA, a sparse variant of LoRA, better preserves alignment safety while maintaining task performance when finetuning LLMs on small datasets.
Empirical analysis shows that classifiers with higher robustness under noise rely more on monosemantic features.
Theoretical analysis on a toy model indicates monosemantic features have better linear separability under noise, leading to more robust decision boundaries.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models often suffer from a lack of interpretability due to polysemanticity, where individual neurons are activated by multiple unrelated semantics, resulting in unclear attributions of model behavior. Recent advances in monosemanticity, where neurons correspond to consistent and distinct semantics, have significantly improved interpretability but are commonly believed to compromise accuracy. In this work, we challenge the prevailing belief of the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff, showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also bring concrete gains in model performance. Across multiple robust learning scenarios-including input and label noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization-our results show that models leveraging monosemantic features significantly outperform those relying on polysemantic features. Furthermore, we provide empirical and theoretical understandings on the robustness gains of feature monosemanticity. Our preliminary analysis suggests that monosemanticity, by promoting better separation of feature representations, leads to more robust decision boundaries. This diverse evidence highlights the generality of monosemanticity in improving model robustness. As a first step in this new direction, we embark on exploring the learning benefits of monosemanticity beyond interpretability, supporting the long-standing hypothesis of linking interpretability and robustness. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/PKU-ML/Beyond_Interpretability}.

papers.title: Which Attention Heads Matter for In-Context Learning?
papers.research_question: Which attention heads (induction heads or function vector heads) are more important for in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Function vector (FV) heads are the primary drivers of few-shot in-context learning performance, especially in larger models, and many FV heads evolve from induction heads during training.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that function vector heads are crucial for in-context learning, challenging the prevailing view that induction heads are the key mechanism, and highlights methodological insights for interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FV heads are more important for few-shot ICL than induction heads, especially in larger models.
Induction heads and FV heads are distinct but correlated.
Many FV heads start as induction heads during training and then transition to the FV mechanism.
The choice of metric (few-shot accuracy vs. token-loss difference) leads to different conclusions about the importance of induction heads.
The relative importance of FV heads increases with model scale.
future_direction: Investigate why induction heads might be necessary precursors to FV heads.
Determine the role of remaining induction heads in fully trained models.
Explore additional mechanisms that could explain ICL capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) capability, enabling them to perform new tasks using only a few demonstrations in the prompt. Two different mechanisms have been proposed to explain ICL: induction heads that find and copy relevant tokens, and function vector (FV) heads whose activations compute a latent encoding of the ICL task. To better understand which of the two distinct mechanisms drives ICL, we study and compare induction heads and FV heads in 12 language models. Through detailed ablations, we discover that few-shot ICL performance depends primarily on FV heads, especially in larger models. In addition, we uncover that FV and induction heads are connected: many FV heads start as induction heads during training before transitioning to the FV mechanism. This leads us to speculate that induction facilitates learning the more complex FV mechanism that ultimately drives ICL.

papers.title: MolReasoner: Toward Effective and Interpretable Reasoning for Molecular LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance across various domains, but their ability to perform molecular reasoning remains underexplored. Existing methods mostly rely on general-purpose prompting, which lacks domain-specific molecular semantics, or fine-tuning, which faces challenges in interpretability and reasoning depth, often leading to structural and textual hallucinations. To address these issues, we introduce MolReasoner, a two-stage framework that transitions LLMs from memorization to high-fidelity chemical reasoning. In the Mol-SFT stage, knowledge-enhanced Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data provides a strong foundation, while the Mol-RL stage refines reasoning using a novel, task-adaptive reward system to mitigate hallucinations. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MolReasoner significantly outperforms a wide range of strong baselines in both molecule generation and captioning tasks. Further analyses highlight the framework's synergistic design and its ability to produce more interpretable outputs. Our work presents a principled and effective new approach for advancing high-fidelity molecular reasoning.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations Learned In-Context by Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models implicitly learn physics during in-context learning, and do recognizable physical quantities emerge as distinct features in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that large language models can learn to forecast physical dynamics via in-context learning, and that energy-related features emerge in their residual stream activations, which are causally important for accurate predictions.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate that LLMs can internalize physical concepts like energy during in-context learning, suggesting transformer architectures can internalize abstract reasoning priors similar to human abstraction.
papers.key_findings:
Prediction accuracy for physical dynamics forecasting improves with longer context length.
Sparse activations from sparse autoencoders (SAEs) applied to residual streams correlate with energy quantities (total, kinetic, potential).
The correlation between sparse activations and energy is context-dependent and increases with longer contexts, especially for chaotic systems.
Intervention experiments ablating energy-correlated sparse activations degrade prediction accuracy, indicating their functional role.
Energy-related features are most prominently captured in the middle layers of the transformer.
papers.limitation: The study uses raw trajectory values as the sole input modality without external instructions or prompting strategies, leaving open whether chain-of-thought or structured prompts would strengthen correlations.
future_direction: Explore physics concepts beyond classical mechanics.
Investigate more human-aligned tasks such as answering conceptual questions from physics exams.
Leverage physics-informed tasks to understand internal mechanisms of large-scale models and advance LLM-based agents for physically realistic environments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) abilities, enabling them to solve wide range of tasks via textual prompts alone. As these capabilities advance, the range of applicable domains continues to expand significantly. However, identifying the precise mechanisms or internal structures within LLMs that allow successful ICL across diverse, distinct classes of tasks remains elusive.
