Physics-based tasks offer a promising testbed for probing this challenge. Unlike synthetic sequences such as basic arithmetic or symbolic equations, physical systems provide experimentally controllable, real-world data based on structured dynamics grounded in fundamental principles. This makes them particularly suitable for studying the emergent reasoning behaviors of LLMs in a realistic yet tractable setting. Here, we mechanistically investigate the ICL ability of LLMs, especially focusing on their ability to reason about physics. Using a dynamics forecasting task in physical systems as a proxy, we evaluate whether LLMs can learn physics in context. We first show that the performance of dynamics forecasting in context improves with longer input contexts. To uncover how such capability emerges in LLMs, we analyze the model's residual stream activations using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Our experiments reveal that the features captured by SAEs correlate with key physical variables, such as energy. These findings demonstrate that meaningful physical concepts are encoded within LLMs during in-context learning. In sum, our work provides a novel case study that broadens our understanding of how LLMs learn in context.

papers.title: Feature Importance Estimation with Self-Attention Networks
papers.research_question: Can attention-based neural networks be used for feature importance estimation in tabular data, and how do they compare to established feature ranking methods?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Self-Attention Networks (SANs) for feature importance estimation in tabular data, showing they perform competitively with established methods and can capture feature interactions.
papers.conclusion: SANs are a viable method for feature importance estimation in tabular data, comparable to existing methods, and can capture feature interactions.
papers.key_findings:
SANs identify similar high-ranked features as established feature ranking methods (ReliefF, Mutual Information, Random Forest).
SANs can detect feature interactions which in some cases yield better predictive performance than baselines.
The attention mechanism in SANs can be used to estimate feature importance directly from the model.
SANs have high space complexity (O(|F|^2) per attention head) which may be a drawback for very high-dimensional data.
On smaller datasets, SANs may not perform as well due to insufficient data for the attention mechanism to distill relevant features.
papers.limitation:
SANs have high space complexity (O(|F|^2) per attention head), which could be prohibitive for very high-dimensional data without sparsity.
SANs may not perform well on small datasets due to insufficient data for the attention mechanism to learn relevant features.
future_direction: Exploring sparsity to reduce the space complexity of SANs.
Comparing SANs with the recently introduced TabNet.
papers.abstract: Black-box neural network models are widely used in industry and science, yet are hard to understand and interpret. Recently, the attention mechanism was introduced, offering insights into the inner workings of neural language models. This paper explores the use of attention-based neural networks mechanism for estimating feature importance, as means for explaining the models learned from propositional (tabular) data. Feature importance estimates, assessed by the proposed Self-Attention Network (SAN) architecture, are compared with the established ReliefF, Mutual Information and Random Forest-based estimates, which are widely used in practice for model interpretation. For the first time we conduct scale-free comparisons of feature importance estimates across algorithms on ten real and synthetic data sets to study the similarities and differences of the resulting feature importance estimates, showing that SANs identify similar high-ranked features as the other methods. We demonstrate that SANs identify feature interactions which in some cases yield better predictive performance than the baselines, suggesting that attention extends beyond interactions of just a few key features and detects larger feature subsets relevant for the considered learning task.

papers.title: Integrating Evolutionary and Compositional Features with ML and DL for Robust and Interpretable Druggable Protein Prediction
papers.research_question: How can evolutionary and compositional features be integrated with machine learning and deep learning for robust and interpretable druggable protein prediction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a hybrid feature representation combining Average Block-based PSSM and Dipeptide Composition for druggable protein prediction, achieving high accuracy with statistical validation and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The hybrid feature representation enables strong predictive performance for druggable protein prediction, with SVM and CapsBiLSTM achieving high accuracy and AUC scores, validated statistically, and providing interpretable insights into sequence descriptors.
papers.key_findings:
Hybrid features (AB-PSSM + DPC) significantly outperform individual descriptors in predicting druggable proteins.
SVM and CapsBiLSTM models achieve classification accuracies above 90% and ROC-AUC/PR-AUC scores above 95%.
Statistical tests (DeLong's test, McNemar's test, bootstrap confidence intervals) confirm the robustness and significance of the improvements.
Interpretability analyses using SHAP and t-SNE reveal biologically significant sequence descriptors influencing druggability.
The proposed framework outperforms existing machine learning and ensemble-based methods in accuracy and interpretability.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Druggable proteins are essential targets in contemporary therapeutic discovery, and their precise identification is necessary for the progression of rational drug design. Traditional biochemical screening techniques are costly, laborious, and protracted, whereas current computational models typically attain only moderate efficacy and seldom offer robust statistical validation or biological interpretability. To mitigate these limitations, we offer a hybrid computational approach that amalgamates evolutionary and compositional information by merging Average Block-based Position-Specific Scoring Matrix (AB-PSSM) characteristics with Dipeptide Composition (DPC) into a 600-dimensional representation. The hybrid feature space was assessed utilizing three machine learning algorithms (support vector machine, random forest, and XGBoost) alongside three deep learning architectures (CapsBiLSTM, ResCapsNetPlus, and ResNet1D) following a rigorous five-fold out-of-fold cross-validation protocol to guarantee fairness and reproducibility. A thorough assessment revealed that the hybrid attributes significantly surpassed individual descriptors, with the SVM and CapsBiLSTM classifiers attaining classification accuracies of 90% and ROC-AUC and PR-AUC values surpassing 95%. The robustness and reliability were further validated by statistical analyses, including DeLong’s test, McNemar’s test, and bootstrap confidence intervals, demonstrating that the observed enhancements were substantial and consistent. Furthermore, interpretability investigations employing SHAP feature attribution and t-SNE visualization underscored biologically significant sequence descriptors as pivotal factors influencing druggability, thus mitigating the "black box" constraint inherent in numerous deep learning methodologies. This study presents a statistically validated, interpretable, and high-performing framework for predicting druggable proteins, which outperforms current machine learning and ensemble-based methods, establishing a clear basis for future applications in precision medicine and drug discovery.

papers.title: Multimodal Task Vectors Enable Many-Shot Multimodal In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How to enable Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) to perform many-shot in-context learning without being limited by context length, by compressing examples into implicit representations (task vectors) in the model's attention heads?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Multimodal Task Vectors (MTV), compact implicit representations of in-context examples stored in attention heads, enabling many-shot multimodal in-context learning without fine-tuning and overcoming context length limitations.
papers.conclusion: MTV enables many-shot multimodal in-context learning, scales with examples, and generalizes to similar tasks without requiring fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
MTV outperforms zero-shot and few-shot ICL on various vision-language tasks.
MTV performance scales with the number of compressed examples (shots and iterations).
MTV can be used alongside explicit few-shot examples, freeing up context length.
MTV attention heads extracted on one task can generalize to similar out-of-domain tasks.
papers.limitation:
MTV requires interleaved LMMs and may not work as well on non-interleaved models.
Computing mean activations requires multiple forward passes, which can be computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: The recent success of interleaved Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) in few-shot learning suggests that in-context learning (ICL) with many examples can be promising for learning new tasks. However, this many-shot multimodal ICL setting has one crucial problem: it is fundamentally limited by the model's context length set at pretraining. The problem is especially prominent in the multimodal domain, which processes both text and images, requiring additional tokens. This motivates the need for a multimodal method to compress many shots into fewer tokens without finetuning. In this work, we enable LMMs to perform multimodal, many-shot in-context learning by leveraging Multimodal Task Vectors (MTV) -- compact implicit representations of in-context examples compressed in the model's attention heads. Specifically, we first demonstrate the existence of such MTV in LMMs and then leverage these extracted MTV to enable many-shot in-context learning for various vision-and-language tasks. Our experiments suggest that MTV can scale in performance with the number of compressed shots and generalize to similar out-of-domain tasks without additional context length for inference. Code: https://github.com/Brandon3964/MultiModal-Task-Vector

papers.title: Why Can GPT Learn In-Context? Language Models Implicitly Perform Gradient Descent as Meta-Optimizers
papers.research_question: What is the working mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) in GPT models? The paper investigates whether ICL can be understood as implicit finetuning, where the attention mechanism performs a form of gradient descent.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent, leading to the understanding that in-context learning is a form of implicit finetuning. Inspired by this, the paper designs a momentum-based attention mechanism that improves performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning can be understood as implicit finetuning via a meta-optimization process, and this understanding can inspire model design, as demonstrated by the momentum-based attention.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer attention has a dual form with gradient descent, which explains in-context learning as implicit finetuning.
Empirical comparisons show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning in terms of predictions, attention outputs, attention weights, and attention to training tokens.
Momentum-based attention, designed by analogy with gradient descent with momentum, improves performance on language modeling and in-context learning tasks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to Transformer-based models and does not consider other architectures.
The dual form is derived using a relaxed linear attention approximation, and the mechanism of standard attention without approximation may be more complex.
Experiments are limited to models up to 2.7B parameters and only classification tasks, leaving larger models and other task types for future work.
future_direction: Study in-context learning for non-Transformer architectures.
Investigate the mechanism of standard Transformer attention without the linear approximation.
Extend the analysis to larger models and other tasks like open-ended generation.
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models have shown surprising in-context learning (ICL) ability. With a few demonstration input-label pairs, they can predict the label for an unseen input without parameter updates. Despite the great success in performance, its working mechanism still remains an open question. In this paper, we explain language models as meta-optimizers and understand in-context learning as implicit finetuning. Theoretically, we figure out that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent. On top of it, we understand ICL as follows: GPT first produces meta-gradients according to the demonstration examples, and then these meta-gradients are applied to the original GPT to build an ICL model. We comprehensively compare the behaviors of in-context learning and explicit finetuning on real tasks to provide empirical evidence that supports our understanding. Experimental results show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning from multiple perspectives. Inspired by the dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, we design a momentum-based attention by analogy with gradient descent with momentum. The improved performance over vanilla attention further supports our understanding from another perspective, and more importantly, shows the potential to utilize our understanding for future model design. The code is available at \url{https://aka.ms/icl}.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
papers.research_question: Whether video-based models rely on factorized representations of physical variables or implicitly represent them in a task-specific, distributed manner, and how physical information is organized within video encoders.
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sharp intermediate-depth transition (Physics Emergence Zone) where physical variables become accessible in video encoders, revealing that models use distributed, task-specific representations rather than factorized, physics-engine-like representations.
papers.conclusion: The findings argue against compact, reusable latent physics states and instead support a distributed, task-specific representational regime, aligning with heuristic-based accounts of intuitive physics.
papers.key_findings:
A Physics Emergence Zone at approximately one-third network depth marks where physical information becomes linearly accessible.
Scalar motion quantities (speed, acceleration magnitude) are available from early layers, while motion direction emerges only at the Physics Emergence Zone.
Direction and possible–impossible physics judgments occupy nearly orthogonal representational subspaces, indicating task-specific representations.
Local spatiotemporal attention heads within the Physics Emergence Zone are causally important for both direction encoding and physics judgments.
Direction is encoded as a high-dimensional population code with circular geometry, requiring coordinated intervention across many dimensions to steer.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to encoder-based video transformers trained with masked objectives; autoregressive or diffusion models may exhibit different representational structure.
Focus on possible–impossible discrimination and controlled motion variables does not isolate richer physical computations such as contact dynamics, force inference, or long-horizon interaction.
Methods characterize representational accessibility and coarse causal influence rather than a complete circuit-level mechanism.
Synthetic toy-ball dataset may not reflect how physical structure is represented in natural video.
papers.abstract: A long-standing question in physical reasoning is whether video-based models need to rely on factorized representations of physical variables in order to make physically accurate predictions, or whether they can implicitly represent such variables in a task-specific, distributed manner. While modern video world models achieve strong performance on intuitive physics benchmarks, it remains unclear which of these representational regimes they implement internally. Here, we present the first interpretability study to directly examine physical representations inside large-scale video encoders. Using layerwise probing, subspace geometry, patch-level decoding, and targeted attention ablations, we characterize where physical information becomes accessible and how it is organized within encoder-based video transformers. Across architectures, we identify a sharp intermediate-depth transition -- which we call the Physics Emergence Zone -- at which physical variables become accessible. Physics-related representations peak shortly after this transition and degrade toward the output layers. Decomposing motion into explicit variables, we find that scalar quantities such as speed and acceleration are available from early layers onwards, whereas motion direction becomes accessible only at the Physics Emergence Zone. Notably, we find that direction is encoded through a high-dimensional population structure with circular geometry, requiring coordinated multi-feature intervention to control. These findings suggest that modern video models do not use factorized representations of physical variables like a classical physics engine. Instead, they use a distributed representation that is nonetheless sufficient for making physical predictions.

papers.title: Interpreting Language Models Through Concept Descriptions: A Survey
papers.research_question: The paper surveys the field of concept descriptions for model components, aiming to answer questions about common methods and data sources, best practices for evaluation, observed trends, and key gaps and future directions.
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions, charting methods, evaluation techniques, and datasets, and identifies a growing demand for rigorous causal evaluation and provides a roadmap for future research.
papers.conclusion: The use of LLMs to generate concept descriptions is a notable step towards demystifying LLMs, with a trajectory from labeling neurons to abstractions and maturing evaluation methods, but the path to verifiable causal mechanisms is not yet fully paved and costs and faithfulness concerns remain.
papers.key_findings:
Recognition of neuron polysemanticity has driven adoption of model abstractions like Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and frameworks for multiple concepts per feature.
Evaluation of concept descriptions is maturing, with multi-faceted metrics assessing predictive power, input accuracy, and causal faithfulness.
The field is moving from labeling individual neurons to higher-level abstractions like SAEs and circuits.
There is a need for more rigorous causal evaluation and standardized benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
Focus limited to natural language concept descriptions for internal model components and abstractions, excluding other interpretability work.
Substantial computational and financial costs associated with the methods surveyed.
Focus on English-language models and text corpora, with generalization to other languages being an open question.
future_direction: Scaling automated description methods to circuits.
Applying concept description methods to new data domains and modalities.
Analyzing the interpreters (LLMs) themselves to understand biases and limitations in generated descriptions.
papers.abstract: Understanding the decision-making processes of neural networks is a central goal of mechanistic interpretability. In the context of Large Language Models (LLMs), this involves uncovering the underlying mechanisms and identifying the roles of individual model components such as neurons and attention heads, as well as model abstractions such as the learned sparse features extracted by Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). A rapidly growing line of work tackles this challenge by using powerful generator models to produce open-vocabulary, natural language concept descriptions for these components. In this paper, we provide the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions. We chart the key methods for generating these descriptions, the evolving landscape of automated and human metrics for evaluating them, and the datasets that underpin this research. Our synthesis reveals a growing demand for more rigorous, causal evaluation. By outlining the state of the art and identifying key challenges, this survey provides a roadmap for future research toward making models more transparent.

papers.title: Understanding and Controlling Repetition Neurons and Induction Heads in In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between repetition neurons and induction heads in in-context learning, and how does their ablation affect ICL performance and repetitive generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a layer-wise analysis showing that repetition neurons in late layers are critical for ICL, while middle-layer neurons can be ablated to reduce repetition without harming ICL, and proposes a three-segment ablation strategy for this purpose.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that repetition neurons and induction heads form a cascade for pattern recognition in ICL, and that selective ablation of middle-layer repetition neurons can reduce repetitive generation while preserving ICL performance.
papers.key_findings:
The impact of repetition neuron ablation on ICL performance varies significantly with layer depth.
Repetition neurons in output-side layers serve as critical executors of pattern-based predictions, with effects on ICL performance comparable to induction heads.
Joint ablation of both repetition neurons and induction heads leads to a near-complete breakdown of pattern recognition.
Selectively deactivating repetition neurons in middle layers reduces repetition while preserving ICL performance.
future_direction: Generalizing the three-step pipeline (behavioral pattern detection, neuron/head ranking, targeted ablation) to other problems like memorization.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between large language models' (LLMs) ability to recognize repetitive input patterns and their performance on in-context learning (ICL). In contrast to prior work that has primarily focused on attention heads, we examine this relationship from the perspective of skill neurons, specifically repetition neurons. Our experiments reveal that the impact of these neurons on ICL performance varies depending on the depth of the layer in which they reside. By comparing the effects of repetition neurons and induction heads, we further identify strategies for reducing repetitive outputs while maintaining strong ICL capabilities.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: Label Words are Anchors: An Information Flow Perspective for Understanding In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work in large language models, specifically what is the role of label words in the information flow?
papers.core_contribution: Label words serve as anchors in in-context learning: they aggregate information from demonstrations in shallow layers and provide reference for predictions in deep layers.
papers.conclusion: Label words function as anchors in ICL, aggregating and distributing task-relevant information; this understanding enables improvements in accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Label words aggregate information from demonstration examples in shallow transformer layers.
The model extracts information from label words in deep layers to form the final prediction.
Anchor re-weighting, which adjusts the significance of label words, improves ICL accuracy by an average of 16.7%.
Compressing demonstrations to anchor hidden states (Hiddenanchor) speeds up inference by up to 1.8× with minimal performance loss.
ICL errors can be diagnosed by analyzing distances between anchor key vectors, which correlate with category confusion.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to classification tasks and does not explore generative tasks.
Due to hardware constraints, models are limited to up to 6 billion parameters, leaving larger-scale models unexplored.
The hypothesis is only examined in conventional ICL paradigms, not in others like chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Replicating the study with larger-scale models.
Exploring other ICL paradigms such as chain-of-thought prompting.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) emerges as a promising capability of large language models (LLMs) by providing them with demonstration examples to perform diverse tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of how LLMs learn from the provided context remains under-explored. In this paper, we investigate the working mechanism of ICL through an information flow lens. Our findings reveal that label words in the demonstration examples function as anchors: (1) semantic information aggregates into label word representations during the shallow computation layers' processing; (2) the consolidated information in label words serves as a reference for LLMs' final predictions. Based on these insights, we introduce an anchor re-weighting method to improve ICL performance, a demonstration compression technique to expedite inference, and an analysis framework for diagnosing ICL errors in GPT2-XL. The promising applications of our findings again validate the uncovered ICL working mechanism and pave the way for future studies.

papers.title: Is This Just Fantasy? Language Model Representations Reflect Human Judgments of Event Plausibility
papers.research_question: How do language models internally represent modal categories (probable, improbable, impossible, inconceivable)? How do these representations develop, do they reflect human categorization behavior, and what interpretable features do they correspond to?
papers.core_contribution: Language models form linear representations (modal difference vectors) that distinguish between modal categories (probable, improbable, impossible, inconceivable). These vectors are more diagnostic than output probabilities, emerge in an intuitive order during training, and reflect fine-grained human categorization behavior and interpretable features like event likelihood and imageability.
papers.conclusion: Language models learn internal representations of modal categories that go beyond output probabilities. These representations develop in an intuitive order and capture nuanced aspects of human categorization, offering a novel way to study world models in LMs and potentially human cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Modal difference vectors within LM hidden states reliably classify sentences by modal category, outperforming classification based on sentence probability.
Modal difference vectors develop in a consistent order: inconceivable vs. others emerges first, followed by probable vs. impossible, then probable vs. improbable, and finally improbable vs. impossible.
Projections of sentences onto modal difference vectors create a feature space that accurately models human participants' graded categorization judgments.
Projections along the impossible-inconceivable vector correlate selectively with human ratings of imageability and the presence of physical objects/places.
Preliminary steering experiments show that adding modal difference vectors to the residual stream during generation can influence the modal category of the generated text.
future_direction: Using modal difference vectors to test the intuitive theories about the world that LMs encode from text.
Using modal difference vectors to generate hypotheses about human representations of modal categories, such as the role of imagination in distinguishing impossible from inconceivable events.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) are used for a diverse range of tasks, from question answering to writing fantastical stories. In order to reliably accomplish these tasks, LMs must be able to discern the modal category of a sentence (i.e., whether it describes something that is possible, impossible, completely nonsensical, etc.). However, recent studies have called into question the ability of LMs to categorize sentences according to modality (Michaelov et al., 2025; Kauf et al., 2023). In this work, we identify linear representations that discriminate between modal categories within a variety of LMs, or modal difference vectors. Analysis of modal difference vectors reveals that LMs have access to more reliable modal categorization judgments than previously reported. Furthermore, we find that modal difference vectors emerge in a consistent order as models become more competent (i.e., through training steps, layers, and parameter count). Notably, we find that modal difference vectors identified within LM activations can be used to model fine-grained human categorization behavior. This potentially provides a novel view into how human participants distinguish between modal categories, which we explore by correlating projections along modal difference vectors with human participants' ratings of interpretable features. In summary, we derive new insights into LM modal categorization using techniques from mechanistic interpretability, with the potential to inform our understanding of modal categorization in humans.

papers.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.
papers.key_findings:
Zero-layer transformers model bigram statistics, accessible directly from weights.
One-layer attention-only transformers are ensembles of bigram and skip-trigram models, enabling simple in-context learning.
Two-layer attention-only transformers implement induction heads through attention head composition, allowing more complex in-context learning.
Induction heads use a sophisticated algorithm to repeat previous sequences based on token similarity.
The framework allows direct analysis of weight matrices to understand model behavior without running the model.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on attention-only transformers, excluding MLP layers which are harder to interpret.
Preliminary and not applied to larger, more complex models.
future_direction: Apply the framework to larger and more realistic models.
Investigate MLP layers in transformers.
papers.abstract: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework? Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning. The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.

papers.title: On Hierarchical Encoding and Reasoning in Deep Transformer-based Generative Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internalize hierarchical structures from data, what is the relationship between this internalization and behaviors like generalization versus memorization, and how can insights into hierarchical reasoning guide the development of more unified, robust, and interpretable multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis investigates how Transformer models learn and represent hierarchical structures, develops methods to probe these structures and mitigate harmful memorization, introduces the PSViT model for hierarchical video prediction, and demonstrates a unified next-frame prediction framework for multimodal tasks.
papers.conclusion: The capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional Transformer models (e.g., BERT) concentrate hierarchical linguistic information near the top layers, while autoregressive/permutation-masked models (e.g., GPT-2, XLNet, Reformer) distribute it more evenly.
Verbatim memorization during fine-tuning is often preceded by a spike in n-gram overlap, which can be used for early-stopping or regularization to reduce leakage by up to 90%.
The PSViT model, designed with hierarchical priors, outperforms latent-space baselines on physical simulation benchmarks, extending accurate prediction horizons by up to 50%.
Abstract physical parameters governing video dynamics are most linearly recoverable from the middle layers of PSViT, mirroring the mid-layer abstraction peak for linguistic hierarchy.
Diverse tasks across text, image, audio, and video can be reformulated into a unified next-frame prediction task, enabling a single PSViT-based model to achieve competitive performance without modality-specific encoders.
papers.limitation:
Probing tasks relied primarily on English datasets (SST, PTB), limiting linguistic diversity.
Memorization experiments used datasets of up to 5,000 samples and greedy decoding; different scales or decoding strategies may alter dynamics.
PSViT was evaluated at 128x128 resolution on deterministic simulations; generalizability to complex real-world video is untested.
The multimodal model was trained separately per task; joint multitask training might better foster shared representations.
future_direction: Extend ancestor probing to morphologically rich languages, different syntactic formalisms, and broader discourse structures.
Scale the n-gram-aware loss regularizer to operate efficiently on hundreds of billions of tokens.
Test PSViT on larger-scale, stochastic, real-world video and integrate differentiable renderers for more direct interpretability.
Explore joint multitask training on a diverse corpus of reformulated multimodal data and richer encodings within the visual canvas.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative Transformer-based foundation models have driven remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, yet their internal mechanisms for representing complex hierarchical structures remain largely unknown, posing significant challenges for interpretability, safety, and robust generalisation. This thesis aims to progress on these issues by systematically investigating how such models internalise hierarchical structures, the relationship between this learning and behaviours like generalisation versus memorisation, and how hierarchical principles can inform the development of safer, more accurate, generative models. To this end, we first introduce novel probing techniques to map the layer-wise emergence of linguistic hierarchies in language models and extend this analysis to the visual domain by developing PSViT: a pixel-space Transformer with hierarchical decompositions of video image patches, shown to learn and generalise hierarchical physical dynamics from raw video data. We investigate memorisation during fine-tuning, establishing an n-gram based early warning signal for verbatim leakage and proposing scalable defences that promote structural generalisation over verbatim memorisation. Building on these insights, we further demonstrate that a unified next-frame prediction framework enables a single model to process text, images, audio, and video without modality-specific encoders, thereby learning shared hierarchical patterns across these diverse inputs. Collectively, our findings underscore that the capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and that a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing
papers.research_question: How are high-level human-interpretable features represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs, and how does the sparsity of these representations vary with model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sparse probing to localize individual neurons representing features in LLMs, revealing that early layers use superposition (sparse combinations of polysemantic neurons), middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons for higher-level features, and model scale increases representational sparsity with varied dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Sparse probing is a powerful tool for understanding feature representation in LLMs, revealing superposition in early layers and monosemantic neurons in middle layers, with scaling effects on sparsity, and opens many directions for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers represent many features in superposition via sparse linear combinations of polysemantic neurons.
Middle layers contain seemingly dedicated (monosemantic) neurons for higher-level contextual features like language or code.
Increasing model scale generally increases representational sparsity, but different features exhibit distinct scaling dynamics.
Sparse probing is an effective method for locating interpretable neurons, even when they are in superposition.
There is a tremendous amount of interpretable structure within the neurons of LLMs, accessible through careful probing and analysis.
papers.limitation:
Interpretation of neurons can be misleading due to 'interpretability illusions' from only examining maximum activating examples.
Conclusive statements about monosemanticity remain methodologically out of reach.
future_direction: Apply sparse probing to other model families and architectures.
Study the dynamics of feature representation during training, not just in final models.
Extend sparse probing to multimodal models and other modalities.
papers.abstract: Despite rapid adoption and deployment of large language models (LLMs), the internal computations of these models remain opaque and poorly understood. In this work, we seek to understand how high-level human-interpretable features are represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs. We train $k$-sparse linear classifiers (probes) on these internal activations to predict the presence of features in the input; by varying the value of $k$ we study the sparsity of learned representations and how this varies with model scale. With $k=1$, we localize individual neurons which are highly relevant for a particular feature, and perform a number of case studies to illustrate general properties of LLMs. In particular, we show that early layers make use of sparse combinations of neurons to represent many features in superposition, that middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons to represent higher-level contextual features, and that increasing scale causes representational sparsity to increase on average, but there are multiple types of scaling dynamics. In all, we probe for over 100 unique features comprising 10 different categories in 7 different models spanning 70 million to 6.9 billion parameters.

papers.title: Towards Universality: Studying Mechanistic Similarity Across Language Model Architectures
papers.research_question: Does mechanistic understanding transfer across different model architectures? Specifically, how similar are the features and circuits in Transformer and Mamba models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer and Mamba models learn similar interpretable features as extracted by Sparse Autoencoders, and their induction circuits are structurally analogous, with a nuanced Off-by-One motif in Mamba.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that SAE feature similarity is a useful measure for cross-architectural universality, revealing significant similarity between Transformer and Mamba features and circuits, with an Off-by-One motif in Mamba.
papers.key_findings:
Most SAE features in Pythia and Mamba are similar, with high Max Pairwise Pearson Correlation (MPPC).
Feature similarity is affected by semantic complexity; simpler features have higher correlation.
Induction circuits in Mamba are analogous to those in Transformers, but with an Off-by-One motif where information is written into the SSM state at the next token.
SAE features show depth specialization across architectures, with matched features appearing at proportionally similar layers.
The neuron baseline shows almost zero similarity, indicating SAEs are better for cross-architecture comparison than neuron-based methods.
papers.limitation:
SAEs may not capture all true features and might capture combinations of features rather than the features themselves.
Circuit universality analysis is qualitative and lacks quantitative automated comparison tools.
future_direction: Automating circuit discovery and comparison for quantitative measurement of circuit universality.
Further study on the Off-by-One motif in Mamba circuits to understand its purpose and formation.
papers.abstract: The hypothesis of Universality in interpretability suggests that different neural networks may converge to implement similar algorithms on similar tasks. In this work, we investigate two mainstream architectures for language modeling, namely Transformers and Mambas, to explore the extent of their mechanistic similarity. We propose to use Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to isolate interpretable features from these models and show that most features are similar in these two models. We also validate the correlation between feature similarity and Universality. We then delve into the circuit-level analysis of Mamba models and find that the induction circuits in Mamba are structurally analogous to those in Transformers. We also identify a nuanced difference we call \emph{Off-by-One motif}: The information of one token is written into the SSM state in its next position. Whilst interaction between tokens in Transformers does not exhibit such trend.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: CoT Vectors: Transferring and Probing the Reasoning Mechanisms of LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we transfer the essence of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning into LLMs in a compact, reusable, and efficient way? Also, how can CoT Vectors be used to probe the underlying mechanisms of reasoning in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge, and proposes Learnable CoT Vectors optimized via a teacher-student framework for more stable and robust guidance.
papers.conclusion: CoT Vectors extend the task vector paradigm to multi-step reasoning, and Learnable CoT Vectors provide stronger and more stable gains, while also serving as a valuable probe into the mechanisms and organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Extracted CoT Vectors show a U-shaped performance curve across layers, revealing a three-stage reasoning process (perception, reasoning, expression) in LLMs.
Learnable CoT Vectors outperform extracted vectors and are more stable across layers.
CoT Vectors achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA while requiring orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters.
The effectiveness of CoT Vectors varies with latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences.
CoT Vectors can be used as a probe to analyze the functional organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Performance variability in intermediate layers highlights structural limitations, suggesting that task-level vectors may not fully capture intra-task diversity.
CoT Vectors can sometimes interfere with correct reasoning paths and lead to incorrect answers, as shown in case studies.
future_direction: Explore finer-grained or adaptive vectorization strategies to improve robustness and generalization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has emerged as a powerful approach to enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing implementations, such as in-context learning and fine-tuning, remain costly and inefficient. To improve CoT reasoning at a lower cost, and inspired by the task vector paradigm, we introduce CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge. Through experiments with Extracted CoT Vectors, we observe pronounced layer-wise instability, manifesting as a U-shaped performance curve that reflects a systematic three-stage reasoning process in LLMs. To address this limitation, we propose Learnable CoT Vectors, optimized under a teacher-student framework to provide more stable and robust guidance. Extensive evaluations across diverse benchmarks and models demonstrate that CoT Vectors not only outperform existing baselines but also achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, while requiring fewer trainable parameters. Moreover, by treating CoT Vectors as a probe, we uncover how their effectiveness varies due to latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences, offering new insights into the functional organization of multi-step reasoning in LLMs. The source code will be released.

papers.title: Sculpting Large Language Models: Probing Structural Asymmetries in Layers and Embedding Spaces
papers.research_question: Whether large language models exhibit internal structural asymmetries and redundancies, and how such structure can be probed and leveraged for model optimization.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a sculpting methodology that reveals structural asymmetries in LLMs, showing that some layers and embedding dimensions are critical while others are redundant, providing insights for model optimization.
papers.conclusion: The findings challenge the notion of homogeneity in LLM components, suggesting they develop internal organization akin to biological or engineered systems, and outline future directions for leveraging this structure.
papers.key_findings:
The first transformer layer is disproportionately critical for model behavior.
Removal of the second half of layers (excluding the last) significantly impairs reasoning tasks.
Removing prime-indexed layers leads to selective degradation, suggesting internal specialization.
The second half of embedding dimensions can be zeroed with minimal performance loss, indicating redundancy.
Odd embedding dimensions are more semantically loaded than even ones, and some alterations (e.g., zeroing a single dimension) can occasionally improve performance, hinting at interference effects.
papers.limitation: The qualitative assessment of model responses (e.g., 'good', 'bad', 'crashed') and the limitations of llama.cpp's output format (e.g., inclusion of tags) constrain the analysis.
future_direction: Scaling up the sculpting approach to larger models (e.g., Mixtral, DeepSeek V3).
Benchmark refinement using granular and domain-specific tasks to uncover functional roles of components.
Exploring the structure of key-value caches to identify knowledge-specific subregions, inspired by DeepSeek V2's Memory Layer Attention (MLA).
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large Language Models (LLMs) are highly complex functions composed of massive parameters organized into layers and embedding dimensions. Yet, whether they exhibit internal structure—akin to biological systems or engineered constructs—remains poorly understood. In this work, we introduce a novel empirical approach to dissect LLM architectures through systematic ablation studies. Our experiments reveal that layers and embedding dimensions are not equal—some of them significantly influence model behavior, while others exhibit redundancy. These findings provide actionable insights for optimizing LLM efficiency and performance. We further propose a sculpting paradigm, wherein strategic modifications to model architecture to locate its internal structure to help to create new state-of-the-art models that both powerful and efficiency.

papers.title: From Neurons to Neutrons: A Case Study in Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability extract scientific knowledge from neural networks trained on physics data, and can such insights align with human-derived domain knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can extract scientifically meaningful representations from neural networks trained on nuclear physics data, aligning with human-derived concepts like the semi-empirical mass formula and shell model.
papers.conclusion: These findings provide a proof-of-concept that neural networks, when trained on scientific data, can learn useful representations that align with human knowledge, opening exciting possibilities for future research on richer data and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings of proton and neutron numbers exhibit a helix structure that encodes nuclear physics concepts like the volume and asymmetry terms.
The orderedness of embeddings along the first principal component correlates with generalization performance.
Penultimate layer features correspond to terms in the semi-empirical mass formula and nuclear shell model.
Latent space topography reveals the algorithm used by the model for binding energy prediction, geometrically representing the SEMF.
Models trained on nuclear data learn representations similar to those trained on pseudo data from human-derived theory.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted knowledge is not guaranteed; representations may be complex and not easily distilled into interpretable theories.
Lack of quantitative metrics to assess interpretability.
Symbolic regression from neural features did not yield fully interpretable improvements over human-derived models.
Requires interdisciplinary collaborations and close partnerships between machine learning researchers and domain experts.
future_direction: Applying interpretability to richer data and more complex tasks.
Developing quantitative metrics for interpretability.
Exploring other scientific domains for knowledge extraction.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) promises a path toward fully understanding how neural networks make their predictions. Prior work demonstrates that even when trained to perform simple arithmetic, models can implement a variety of algorithms (sometimes concurrently) depending on initialization and hyperparameters. Does this mean neuron-level interpretability techniques have limited applicability? We argue that high-dimensional neural networks can learn low-dimensional representations of their training data that are useful beyond simply making good predictions. Such representations can be understood through the mechanistic interpretability lens and provide insights that are surprisingly faithful to human-derived domain knowledge. This indicates that such approaches to interpretability can be useful for deriving a new understanding of a problem from models trained to solve it. As a case study, we extract nuclear physics concepts by studying models trained to reproduce nuclear data.

papers.title: Identifying Functionally Important Features with End-to-End Sparse Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can we identify functionally important features in neural networks? The paper investigates whether standard sparse autoencoders (SAEs) learn features that are functionally important for network performance and proposes a new training method to ensure the features are functionally important.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces end-to-end sparse dictionary learning, a method for training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) that ensures the learned features are functionally important by minimizing the KL divergence between the output distributions of the original model and the model with SAE activations inserted.
papers.conclusion: End-to-end sparse dictionary learning offers a Pareto improvement over standard SAEs, requiring fewer features to explain network performance without sacrificing interpretability, bringing us closer to methods that can explain network behavior concisely and accurately.
papers.key_findings:
For the same level of performance explained, end-to-end SAEs require activating more than twice as few features per datapoint compared to standard SAEs.
End-to-end SAEs require fewer total features over the dataset to explain the same amount of network performance.
End-to-end SAEs with downstream reconstruction loss (SAEe2e+ds) achieve similar performance to SAEe2e while having activations that follow more similar pathways through the network compared to the original model.
The improved efficiency of end-to-end SAEs does not come at the cost of interpretability, as measured by automated interpretability scores and qualitative analysis.
End-to-end SAEs have more orthogonal features and are less prone to feature splitting compared to standard SAEs.
papers.limitation:
End-to-end SAEs take 2-3.5 times longer to train than standard SAEs.
There is a risk that SAEe2e may take different computational pathways through the network, though this is addressed by SAEe2e+ds.
The automated interpretability score is an imperfect metric of interpretability.
future_direction: Using training tweaks such as a sparsity schedule to allow for higher learning rates.
Using locally trained SAEs as initializations to reduce training time.
Training multiple SAEs at different layers concurrently to reduce training time.
papers.abstract: Identifying the features learned by neural networks is a core challenge in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which learn a sparse, overcomplete dictionary that reconstructs a network's internal activations, have been used to identify these features. However, SAEs may learn more about the structure of the datatset than the computational structure of the network. There is therefore only indirect reason to believe that the directions found in these dictionaries are functionally important to the network. We propose end-to-end (e2e) sparse dictionary learning, a method for training SAEs that ensures the features learned are functionally important by minimizing the KL divergence between the output distributions of the original model and the model with SAE activations inserted. Compared to standard SAEs, e2e SAEs offer a Pareto improvement: They explain more network performance, require fewer total features, and require fewer simultaneously active features per datapoint, all with no cost to interpretability. We explore geometric and qualitative differences between e2e SAE features and standard SAE features. E2e dictionary learning brings us closer to methods that can explain network behavior concisely and accurately. We release our library for training e2e SAEs and reproducing our analysis at https://github.com/ApolloResearch/e2e_sae

papers.title: Does TabPFN Understand Causal Structures?
papers.research_question: Does TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model, encode causal knowledge in its internal representations beyond statistical correlations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and introduces an adapter framework that can extract this information for causal discovery, outperforming traditional statistical methods.
papers.conclusion: TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and the proposed adapter framework can extract this information for causal discovery, establishing a new direction for interpretable and adaptable tabular foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Causal information is concentrated in the middle layers (4-6) of TabPFN's encoder.
The proposed framework extracts causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and outperforms statistical baselines (GIES, IGSP, DCDI) on ROC AUC, performing closely to the specialized neural causal discovery model A VICI.
The decoder architecture is crucial for performance; using a learnable decoder significantly improves results compared to using no decoder.
Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, particularly for dense graph structures like Erdős-Rényi and Stochastic Block Model graphs.
Using embeddings from the pre-trained TabPFN encoder (optimal weights) yields better causal discovery performance than using randomly initialized or degraded encoder weights.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, and the approach is sensitive to the type of graph structure.
future_direction: Leveraging pre-trained tabular models for extracting causal structures and improving their interpretability.
Understanding how tabular foundation models reason about different datasets.
Repurposing tabular foundation models for different downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Causal discovery is fundamental for multiple scientific domains, yet extracting causal information from real world data remains a significant challenge. Given the recent success on real data, we investigate whether TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model pre-trained on synthetic datasets generated from structural causal models, encodes causal information in its internal representations. We develop an adapter framework using a learnable decoder and causal tokens that extract causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and decode them into adjacency matrices for causal discovery. Our evaluations demonstrate that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, outperforming several traditional causal discovery algorithms, with such causal information being concentrated in mid-range layers. These findings establish a new direction for interpretable and adaptable foundation models and demonstrate the potential for leveraging pre-trained tabular models for causal discovery.

papers.title: Sparse Modular Activation for Efficient Sequence Modeling
papers.research_question: Can neural networks learn to activate their attention modules on demand to achieve better quality-efficiency trade-off? How much extra attention is needed for the SSMs on a task-by-task basis?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Modular Activation (SMA), a general mechanism for sparsely and dynamically activating sub-modules in neural networks, and applies it to design SeqBoat, a novel hybrid SSM-GAU architecture that achieves significantly better quality-efficiency trade-offs in sequence modeling.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Modular Activation (SMA) enables efficient and interpretable dynamic module activation, and its application in SeqBoat demonstrates superior quality-efficiency trade-offs across diverse sequence modeling tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SeqBoat achieves new state-of-the-art average accuracy among linear-complexity hybrid models on the Long Range Arena (LRA) benchmark.
SeqBoat provides substantial training speedup and memory reduction compared to Transformer and other baselines, e.g., 10.4x speedup and 95% memory reduction on the LRA Text task.
The learned sparse activation patterns of the GAU module directly reveal the amount of attention needed for each task and data sample.
The working memory mechanism in SeqBoat enables linear inference complexity with theoretically infinite attention span and outperforms chunking-based models.
SeqBoat achieves competitive performance on speech classification (Speech Commands) and language modeling (enwik8) with improved efficiency.
papers.limitation:
The current implementation of SMA is I/O bounded due to copying large tensors with scatter operations, and no custom fused kernels were used for memory bandwidth optimization.
Experiments were limited to models of moderate size due to computational resource constraints, leaving scalability to larger models uncertain.
future_direction: Explore the scaling behavior of SMA and how to incorporate it with pre-trained large language models.
Investigate the interpretability of module activation patterns and their correlation with input tokens or model predictions.
Scale up SMA with a large number of modules, potentially impacting Mixture-of-Experts research.
papers.abstract: Recent hybrid models combining Linear State Space Models (SSMs) with self-attention mechanisms have demonstrated impressive results across a range of sequence modeling tasks. However, current approaches apply attention modules statically and uniformly to all elements in the input sequences, leading to sub-optimal quality-efficiency trade-offs. To address this limitation, we introduce Sparse Modular Activation (SMA), a general mechanism enabling neural networks to sparsely and dynamically activate sub-modules for sequence elements in a differentiable manner. Through allowing each element to skip non-activated sub-modules, SMA reduces computation and memory consumption of neural networks at both training and inference stages. To validate the effectiveness of SMA on sequence modeling, we design a novel neural architecture, SeqBoat, which employs SMA to sparsely activate a Gated Attention Unit (GAU) based on the state representations learned from an SSM. By constraining the GAU to only conduct local attention on the activated inputs, SeqBoat can achieve linear inference complexity with theoretically infinite attention span, and provide substantially better quality-efficiency trade-off than the chunking-based models. With experiments on a wide range of tasks, including long sequence modeling, speech classification and language modeling, SeqBoat brings new state-of-the-art results among hybrid models with linear complexity, and reveals the amount of attention needed for each task through the learned sparse activation patterns. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/renll/SeqBoat.

papers.title: Sparsification and Reconstruction from the Perspective of Representation Geometry
papers.research_question: How does sparse encoding organize the representations of activation vectors from language models? What is the relationship between this organizational paradigm and feature disentanglement as well as reconstruction performance?
papers.core_contribution: This study explains the principles of sparsity from the perspective of representational geometry and demonstrates the impact of changes in representational structure on reconstruction performance, emphasizing the necessity of understanding representations and incorporating representational constraints.
papers.conclusion: The findings offer guidance for improving SAEs and developing novel tools for decomposing neural networks from the perspective of representation geometry, particularly emphasizing the necessity of understanding and incorporating representation geometry constraints.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs exhibit stratified manifolds where representations of the same concept are distributed across different manifolds.
Sparse encoding reduces feature overlap by merging similar semantic features within local representations and introducing more dimensionality, achieving feature disentanglement.
Increased separability between different local representations causally enhances reconstruction performance in SAEs.
The variability of the feature modal rank (r3) and AGD under noise validates the stratified structure of representations.
Global representations are compressed during sparse encoding, while local representations gain effective dimensionality and connected components.
papers.limitation:
Extraction of activations depends on prompts related to the concept, not guaranteeing all representations are captured.
Regularization in SAEs is not included as a controlled variable, and differences in representation structure caused by variations in regularization require further exploration.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a predominant tool in mechanistic interpretability, aiming to identify interpretable monosemantic features. However, how does sparse encoding organize the representations of activation vector from language models? What is the relationship between this organizational paradigm and feature disentanglement as well as reconstruction performance? To address these questions, we propose the SAEMA, which validates the stratified structure of the representation by observing the variability of the rank of the symmetric semipositive definite (SSPD) matrix corresponding to the modal tensor unfolded along the latent tensor with the level of noise added to the residual stream. To systematically investigate how sparse encoding alters representational structures, we define local and global representations, demonstrating that they amplify inter-feature distinctions by merging similar semantic features and introducing additional dimensionality. Furthermore, we intervene the global representation from an optimization perspective, proving a significant causal relationship between their separability and the reconstruction performance. This study explains the principles of sparsity from the perspective of representational geometry and demonstrates the impact of changes in representational structure on reconstruction performance. Particularly emphasizes the necessity of understanding representations and incorporating representational constraints, providing empirical references for developing new interpretable tools and improving SAEs. The code is available at \hyperlink{https://github.com/wenjie1835/SAERepGeo}{https://github.com/wenjie1835/SAERepGeo}.

papers.title: Investigating the Encoding of Words in BERT’s Neurons Using Feature Textualization
papers.research_question: Can the knowledge encoded in individual neurons of BERT be interpreted and symbolized as words, and how many neurons are needed to encode words?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces feature textualization, an adaptation of activation maximization for language models, and uses it to show that single neurons in BERT do not encode words, but groups of 250-450 neurons can be associated with word-like representations.
papers.conclusion: Feature textualization can reveal information encoded in groups of neurons in language models, showing that single neurons do not encode words but groups of 250-450 neurons can be associated with word-like representations.
papers.key_findings:
Words only utilize about 3% of the theoretical activation potential of single neurons, indicating word-based interpretations are not faithful.
Optimized inputs for single neurons are not semantically similar to word embeddings (average cosine similarity ~0.124).
For groups of 250-450 neurons, optimized inputs become similar to word embeddings (cosine similarity ~0.26) and the target word is the closest word in 67% of cases.
Feature textualization can reveal the information encoded in groups of neurons, helping to locate encoded knowledge in model parameters.
The method is computationally expensive and currently infeasible for very large language models.
papers.limitation:
The method is computationally expensive and infeasible for very large language models.
The interpretations are model-specific and do not generalize.
Non-regularized optimal inputs might be adversarial and lie in uninterpretable parts of the vector space.
future_direction: Investigate what high-level semantic knowledge is encoded within neurons, beyond word-level interpretations.
Develop regularizers to pull optimized inputs towards the populated part of the word embedding space.
Apply the method to other language models, including fine-tuned or larger models, and investigate contextualized inputs.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (PLMs) form the basis of most state-of-the-art NLP technologies. Nevertheless, they are essentially black boxes: Humans do not have a clear understanding of what knowledge is encoded in different parts of the models, especially in individual neurons. A contrast is in computer vision, where feature visualization provides a decompositional interpretability technique for neurons of vision models. Activation maximization is used to synthesize inherently interpretable visual representations of the information encoded in individual neurons. Our work is inspired by this but presents a cautionary tale on the interpretability of single neurons, based on the first large-scale attempt to adapt activation maximization to NLP, and, more specifically, large PLMs. We propose feature textualization, a technique to produce dense representations of neurons in the PLM word embedding space. We apply feature textualization to the BERT model to investigate whether the knowledge encoded in individual neurons can be interpreted and symbolized. We find that the produced representations can provide insights about the knowledge encoded in individual neurons, but that individual neurons do not represent clear-cut symbolic units of language such as words. Additionally, we use feature textualization to investigate how many neurons are needed to encode words in BERT.

papers.title: Is Random Attention Sufficient for Sequence Modeling? Disentangling Trainable Components in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How much, and which aspects, of transformer performance gains can be attributed to the self-attention mechanism, and which degrees of freedom inside the Transformer are truly necessary for its behaviors?
